# FSA Rollovers vs. Grace Periods


Ben Luthi · November 27, 2026 · 8 min read


A Flexible Spending Account (FSA) offers employees the chance to save for medical expenses pre-tax.Because contributions come out of your paycheck before taxes, an FSA lowers your taxable income. In most cases, you need to use your FSA funds by the end of the plan year.


That is, unless your plan has an[FSA rollover](https://livelyme.com/blog/flexible-spending-account-fsa-rollover) or grace period. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)[allows employers to opt in](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) to one of these options. Both help employees who have money left in their FSA at the end of the year.


Here's how each option works, how they compare, and what happens to your FSA balance at the end of the plan year.


## Which Types of FSAs Can Roll Over?


There are three different types of FSA plans you can get. These plans are only available through employers that offer them. In each case, your contributions come out of your paycheck before federal income and payroll taxes, which lowers your taxable income.


Here's a look at each different type of FSA:


-


**General Purpose or Healthcare FSA** : You can use funds for eligible medical expenses, including dental and vision. Eligible people include you, your spouse and any dependents you claim on your tax return. A[healthcare FSA](https://livelyme.com/blog/what-is-a-healthcare-fsa) can offer a rollover or a grace period.


-


**Dependent Care FSA** : Participants can use money from this account to pay for dependent care of a child or adult. It's intended for individuals who need dependent care so they can work.[Dependent Care FSAs](https://livelyme.com/blog/what-is-a-dependent-care-fsa) don’t offer a rollover option, but may offer a grace period or run-out period.


-


**Limited-Purpose FSA** : This FSA only includes qualifying dental and vision expenses.[Limited-purpose FSAs](https://livelyme.com/blog/what-is-a-limited-purpose-fsa) can come with a rollover or a grace period.


For 2026, you can contribute up to $3,400 to a healthcare or limited-purpose FSA, and up to $3,500 for plan years beginning in 2027. The dependent care FSA limit is $7,500 per household, or $3,750 if you're married and file separately. Your employer can set a lower limit. See the full[FSA contribution limits](https://livelyme.com/blog/fsa-contribution-limits) .


Healthcare and limited purpose FSAs are not like HSAs - they work with any health insurance plan and you do not have to have a[qualified high-deductible health plan](https://livelyme.com/guides/hdhp) to use them.


As such, they’re perfect if your health insurance plan doesn’t qualify for an HSA.


## How do rollovers and grace periods work?


The default setting for FSAs is the "Use It or Lose It" rule. This means you give up any FSA funds you don’t spend by the end of the plan year.[HSAs work differently](https://livelyme.com/guides/hsa-guide) . With an HSA, unused money stays in your account from year to year.


The IRS gives employers two options that help limit that loss for employees with money left in a healthcare FSA or limited-purpose FSA.


Employers that offer these FSAs can choose to offer a rollover, grace period or nothing at all. The only catch is that they can’t offer more than one option. Employers can also offer a run-out period, which gives you extra time to submit claims for the previous year's expenses.


### FSA rollover


The IRS sets the rollover limit for FSAs each year. With an FSA rollover, participants can carry over up to $680 of unused 2026 funds into[2027](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf) and up to $700 of unused 2027 funds into[2028](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/irs-releases-tax-inflation-adjustments-for-tax-year-2027-taxpayers-continue-to-benefit-from-the-working-families-tax-cuts) .


Let's take this real life example:


You have a $750 balance at the end of 2026. In 2027, you can start the year off with $680 plus that year's FSA contribution limit. While you did have more money in your FSA left over, you're only allowed to take up to the rollover limit into the next year.


If you have less than the carryover amount remaining in your account, you can roll over the full FSA balance. What’s more, you can still contribute the maximum amount in the following year.


### Grace period


With the grace period option, employees get u[p to 2 months and 15 days after the plan year ends](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) to use the previous year's FSA funds. For a plan year that ends December 31, the deadline is March 15. As long as the service occurs within that grace period, it qualifies.


There’s no limit on how much you can use during an FSA grace period. This means it can be more beneficial if you have more funds than the carryover limit.


### Run-out period


A run-out period is a period of time during your new plan year in which you can still file claims for expenses made in the previous year.


Let's say your run-out period lasts until March 31. You will have until then to file a claim for FSA funds for any eligible expense made by December 31 of the previous year. This can be helpful because there’s often a delay between your service or procedure and when you get your bill.

As an employee, you don't get to choose which FSA extension option you get.Your employer chooses, and it may choose not to offer either one.


Depending on the situation, you may have some influence in the decision-making process for future FSA plan years. So it’s a good idea to understand both options and their benefits and drawbacks. If your plan doesn't offer either option, you can ask HR whether it would consider adding one.


### Rollover pros and cons


The biggest benefit to an FSA rollover is that you’ll have the entire upcoming plan year to use the funds from the previous year. This setup is helpful if you don’t have any medical services or procedures scheduled at the beginning of the following year.


The downside is that you can only roll over up to the maximum carryover amount. Of you have more than that in unused funds, you’ll still be leaving some money on the table, even if not the full amount.


### Grace period pros and cons


The grace period option doesn’t limit how much of the previous plan year’s unused funds you can use. As long as you incur the expense within the first 2.5 months of the following plan year, you can get reimbursed.


That said, the amount of time you have to use your FSA funds is much shorter than with the rollover alternative. If you aren’t proactive about using it all at the beginning of the year, you may still lose some of it.


## Other tips for using your FSA money


Make it a goal to use your entire FSA balance by the deadline. Here are a few options to consider:


-


**Know what qualifies** : The IRS lists eligible medical expenses in[Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) and qualified dependent care expenses in[Publication 50](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p503) **3** . Check both lists against expenses you've already had this year. Remember that if you have a limited-purpose FSA, your options are limited in comparison to a healthcare FSA.


-


**Check What's Eligible:** Lively's[What's Eligible](https://livelyme.com/whats-eligible) page shows which products and services qualify for FSA and HSA funds, so you can plan purchases before your deadline.


One thing to avoid is prepaying for medical care that will not happen during the plan year or grace period. An expense isn’t considered incurred unless the actual service occurs during the account’s plan year. If you try to use your FSA funds to pay for care in advance, it may not be eligible for reimbursement.


## The bottom line


The FSA rollover and grace period offer relief to account holders at the end of the year. If you have an FSA, your employer gets to choose which one to offer, and it may not give you either option.


Speak with your HR representative to find out what your employer offers. Regardless of which option they chose, it’s important to be mindful of your account balance. It’s also important to have a plan to use all the money before the deadline. You’ll be able to maximize the value your FSA offers without the stress of trying to catch up the following year.


If you do have unused FSA money at the end of the year, consider adjusting your contributions. This way, you may be able to avoid having a surplus of funds in the upcoming year.


FSA Rollover and Grace Period FAQs


### Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


Does an FSA roll over?


Only if your employer's plan offers a rollover, also called a carryover. For plan years beginning in 2026, you can carry over up to $680 into 2027. Without a rollover or grace period, unused funds are forfeited after the plan year and any run-out period.


Can an employer offer both a rollover and a grace period?


No. A healthcare FSA can offer a rollover or a grace period, but not both.


Does a dependent care FSA roll over?


No. A dependent care FSA can't offer a rollover, but it can offer a grace period.


Does a limited-purpose FSA roll over?


It can. A limited-purpose FSA can offer a rollover or a grace period, the same as a healthcare FSA, if your employer chooses to.
